source_refs.note: Book p. 59-60: 2.12 Differentials, definition dy = f'(x)dx and Example 24

blocks.text: Assume that \(f\) is differentiable at a point \(x\), if \(dx\) is an independent variable that can take values in the neighborhood of 0 and not 0, then we define dependent variable \(dy\), by the formula:

blocks.text_alt: d y equals f prime of x times d x, equation (1)

blocks.text: Since \(dx \ne 0\), we can divide both sides of (1) by \(dx\) to obtain:

blocks.text_alt: d y over d x equals f prime of x

blocks.text: This achieves our goal of defining \(dy\) and \(dx\) so that their ratio is equal to the derivative \(f'(x)\).

Until now \(\frac{dy}{dx}\) was one symbol, the derivative. Here \(dx\) and \(dy\) get their own meaning:
\(dx\) (the differential of \(x\)) is any small non-zero number we choose: the step in \(x\).
\(dy\) (the differential of \(y\)) is then calculated: \(dy = f'(x)\,dx\), slope times step.
In the picture, \(dy\) is how much the tangent line rises when we move \(dx\) along the \(x\)-axis. The next topic (2.12.1) shows that this is very nearly the rise of the curve itself.
blocks.title: Teaching note

blocks.text:
How to find a differential: differentiate as usual, then write \(dx\) after the derivative.
Example: \(y = x^{2}\) gives \(dy = 2x\,dx\); \(y = \sin x\) gives \(dy = \cos x\,dx\).
blocks.title: Teaching note
Example 24
blocks.problem:
(a) Find \(dy\) if \(y = x^{4} + 7x\).
(b) Find the value of \(dy\) when \(x = 1\) and \(dx = 0.1\).
steps:
Given: \(y = x^{4} + 7x\); in (b) \(x = 1\), \(dx = 0.1\).
To find: (a) \(dy\) as a formula; (b) its value.
Method: the definition \(dy = f'(x)\,dx\). First find \(f'(x)\), then multiply by \(dx\).

(a) Step 1: Differentiate
\[f(x) = x^{4} + 7x\]
\[f'(x) = 4x^{3} + 7 \quad \text{...(1)}\]
Why: power rule on each term: \(\frac{d}{dx}x^{4} = 4x^{3}\), \(\frac{d}{dx}7x = 7\).

Step 2: Write the differential
\[dy = f'(x)\,dx\]
\[dy = (4x^{3} + 7)\,dx \quad \text{...(2)}\]
Why: by definition, \(dy\) is the derivative multiplied by \(dx\).

(b) Step 3: Substitute \(x = 1\), \(dx = 0.1\) in (2)
\[dy = (4(1)^{3} + 7)(0.1)\]
\[= 11(0.1) = 1.1\]
Why: \(dy\) depends on two numbers: the point \(x\) and the step \(dx\).

Check:
Dividing (2) by \(dx\) gives \(\frac{dy}{dx} = 4x^{3} + 7\), the derivative, as the definition requires. At \(x = 1\) the slope is 11, and \(11 \times 0.1 = 1.1\).

blocks.text:
1. \(dx\) is an independent small non-zero number; \(dy = f'(x)\,dx\) depends on both \(x\) and \(dx\).
2. Dividing by \(dx\) gives back \(\frac{dy}{dx} = f'(x)\).
3. To find \(dy\): differentiate, then multiply by \(dx\).
4. A numerical value of \(dy\) needs both the point \(x\) and the step \(dx\).
blocks.title: Key points

blocks.text:
1. Forgetting \(dx\): \(dy = 4x^{3} + 7\) is wrong; that is \(\frac{dy}{dx}\).
2. Putting the value of \(dx\) in place of \(x\) (or the other way round) when finding a value.
blocks.title: Common mistake
